lead: Close a thin wall into a loop and twist it, and the torque is carried by a shear flow q that is the same in every wall. This is the Bredt–Batho result, q = T/2A. The stress in each wall is q/t, and the rate of twist depends on the enclosed area and on ∮ds/t. Wing boxes, fuselage barrels and tail booms are sized for torsion this way.
prereq: You need: shear flow q = τ t from the first chapter, and the shear modulus G.

sections.h3: Constant shear flow round a closed loop

blocks.text: Take a single-cell tube under a pure torque T, with no axial load. Cut out a small rectangle of wall bounded by two cross-sections and two lines along the beam. With no direct stress, axial equilibrium of the rectangle needs the shear flows on its two longitudinal edges to be equal. So q does not change along the wall: in a single closed cell under pure torque, q is constant all round, whatever the wall thickness.

Now take moments about any point O. A length ds of wall carries a force q ds, and its moment arm about O is the perpendicular distance p. But p ds is twice the area of the thin triangle from O to the element. Going round the loop, ∮p ds = 2A, so T = 2Aq.
q = T/(2A),   τ = q/t = T/(2A t)
blocks.where: q is the shear flow (N/mm); T is the torque (N·mm); A is the area enclosed by the wall mid-line (mm²); t is the local wall thickness (mm); τ is the shear stress (N/mm²), largest where the wall is thinnest.

blocks.text: Use the area inside the mid-line, not the outer outline. The result assumes a thin wall, free warping of the cross-section ends and an unbuckled skin.

sections.h3: Rate of twist and the torsion constant

blocks.text: The section rotates by θ about its centre of twist. A wall element at perpendicular distance p from that centre moves a distance pθ along the wall, and the shear strain is γ = q/(G t). Summing the work of the shear flow round the loop (or the displacements, which gives the same result) leads to:

blocks.where: dθ/dz is the rate of twist (rad/mm); G is the shear modulus (N/mm²); ∮ds/t is dimensionless (a length over a length) and is summed wall by wall when t changes.

blocks.text: J = 4A²/∮(ds/t),   dθ/dz = T/(G J),   θ = T L/(G J)
blocks.where: J is the torsion constant of the closed section (mm⁴); L is the length of the member (mm); θ is the total twist (rad).

blocks.text: For a circular tube of mean radius R and thickness t, A = πR² and ∮ds/t = 2πR/t, so J = 2πR³t, the polar second moment of a thin ring. The first form of dθ/dz, with q inside the integral, is the one to use for multi-cell sections and for the zero-twist condition of the closed-section shear chapter, where q is not constant.

items: Draw the mid-line and compute A inside it.
Split the loop where t changes and add each length over its own thickness: ∮ds/t = Σ L<sub>i</sub>/t<sub>i</sub>.
q = T/2A in every wall; τ<sub>i</sub> = q/t<sub>i</sub>.
J = 4A²/∮ds/t; dθ/dz = T/GJ; θ = T L/GJ.

blocks.text: The result becomes inaccurate rather than failing outright as the wall thickens, because the stress is no longer uniform through t. Where the cross-section is prevented from warping, at a root rib or a fuselage frame, direct stresses appear and the member is stiffer than the formula says. A wing box with more than one cell has a different q in each cell; the next chapter handles it.

spec.aria: A wide rectangle, 600 by 200 millimetres, with thin top and bottom skins and thicker side webs, shaded inside and labelled A equals 120,000 square millimetres. Arrows run anticlockwise round all four walls. Labels give the stress as 83.3 newtons per square millimetre in each 1.5 millimetre skin and 41.7 in each 3 millimetre web. Below, the integral of ds over t is 933.3, J is 6.171 times ten to the seven, and the twist rate is 1.03 degrees per metre.

examples.question: A single-cell wing box has a rectangular mid-line 600 mm × 200 mm. The top and bottom skins are 1.5 mm thick and the two spar webs 3 mm. It carries T = 30 kN·m. With G = 27 GPa, find q, the stress in the skins and webs, J, the rate of twist and the twist over a 4 m length.
steps: q = T/2A = 30 × 10⁶/(2 × 120,000) = 125.0 N/mm, the same in all four walls.
Skins: τ = 125.0/1.5 = 83.3 N/mm². Webs: τ = 125.0/3 = 41.7 N/mm². The thin skins carry the higher stress.
examples.answer: q = 125 N/mm; τ = 83.3 N/mm² in the skins and 41.7 N/mm² in the webs; J = 6.171 × 10⁷ mm⁴; 1.03° per metre, 4.13° over 4 m.

traps: Using the outside outline for A. A is enclosed by the mid-line.
Taking ∮ds/t as perimeter over the thinnest wall. In the example that gives J = 5.40 × 10⁷ mm⁴ instead of 6.17 × 10⁷, so the twist comes out 14 per cent too large. Add each wall separately.
Assuming the stress is largest in the thick spar webs. q is constant, so τ = q/t is largest in the thinnest wall.
Applying q = T/2A to an open section. With no closed loop there is no enclosed area; open walls follow the St Venant law.
Leaving T in kN·m with A in mm². Convert T to N·mm first.

quiz.q: State the Bredt–Batho formula and define each symbol.
quiz.a: q = T/2A: q the shear flow (N/mm), T the torque (N·mm), A the area enclosed by the wall mid-line (mm²).

quiz.q: Why is q the same in every wall of a single closed cell under pure torque?
quiz.a: With no direct stress, axial equilibrium of any rectangular wall element needs the shear flows on its two longitudinal edges to be equal, so q cannot change along the wall, even where t changes.

quiz.q: A closed tube has A = 50,000 mm², t = 1.5 mm and T = 12 kN·m. Find q and τ.
The same tube has a 1000 mm perimeter and G = 27,000 N/mm². Find J and the twist per metre.
Show that a thin circular tube has J = 2πR³t.
A designer doubles the spar web thickness of the example box and leaves the skins alone. What happens to q, to the skin stress and to the twist?
quiz.a: q = T/2A is unchanged (125 N/mm), so the skin stress stays 83.3 N/mm². ∮ds/t falls to 800 + 66.67 = 866.67, so J rises by 1.077 times and the twist falls by about 7 per cent. Thickening the skins would help both.

beyond: Not for the exam. Composite skins have a shear stiffness that depends on lay-up, so G t replaces G and t in the integral. Search for "torsion of thin-walled closed sections with warping restraint".
